routes.description: Establish sufficient warrant for Christianity by defending appropriate historical and relational modes of inquiry, the credibility of the Gospel portrayal of Jesus, the resurrection inference, and Christianity's account of moral meaning and human value.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative case gives adequate reason to trust the central Christian claims, especially Jesus's identity and resurrection, while showing that documentary, scientific, moral, and rival-religion objections do not defeat that warrant.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defended evidence for Jesus and the resurrection, together with Christianity's explanatory claims, to sufficient warrant for Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Justify using historical, documentary, and relational reasoning without treating scientific repeatability as the sole avenue to truth.
Establish that the Gospel sources preserve a sufficiently coherent and historically credible portrayal of Jesus.
Show that the reported death, empty tomb, appearances, and witness transformation are better explained by resurrection than by relevant alternatives.
Explain objective morality, human value, suffering, and human wrongdoing within a coherent Christian account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify criteria intended to distinguish Christian claims from incompatible religious claims rather than validating them symmetrically.
Distinguish Christianity's normative commitments from disputed interpretations, divine accommodation, and human misuse of scripture.

routes.description: Show that Christianity has not met its burden because its verification methods do not reliably distinguish truth from fiction or rival religions, its sources do not establish their supernatural claims, and its accounts of morality and human value face viable secular alternatives and textual objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proffered methods and evidence remain insufficient to establish the Gospel and resurrection claims, especially when tested against ordinary evidential standards, alternative explanations, internal disputes, and the distinction between transmission and truth.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved evidential and explanatory deficits to withholding affirmation that Christianity is true or sufficiently warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require truth-testing criteria that discriminate Christianity from incompatible religions, fiction, and unsupported supernatural explanations.
Separate textual preservation, consistency, and accurate background details from evidence that the Gospel claims correspond to reality.
Show that resurrection testimony and proposed historical facts do not justify a supernatural bodily-resurrection inference.
Test claims about divine moral grounding and equal human value against secular accounts and morally difficult biblical provisions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that identifying defects in an affirmative method does not require supplying a method that verifies supernatural claims.
Apply empirical scrutiny to asserted physical events even when those events are presented through historical or religious narratives.

sections.title: Truth-Testing Methods and Evidential Burdens
sections.rationale: This issue governs what would count as sufficient warrant, whether Christianity can be distinguished from rival claims, and whether criticism of an offered method incurs a separate positive burden.

sections.title: Gospel Preservation, Coherence, and Historical Reliability
sections.rationale: The Gospel documents are the principal route to claims about Jesus, so the distinction between textual transmission, literary and archaeological indicators, narrative coherence, and factual truth is central.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: The resurrection is presented as Christianity's decisive truth condition, making the death, burial, empty tomb, appearances, witnesses, narrative disagreements, and natural or supernatural explanations the largest issue.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Human Value, and Meaning
sections.rationale: The motion expressly concerns moral meaning and human value, requiring comparison of the proposed divine grounding with secular sources of meaning and moral regard.

sections.title: Scriptural Morality, Creation, Evil, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Claims about creation, gender, slavery, suffering, interpretation, accommodation, and free will test whether Christianity's texts and moral framework remain coherent with its account of divine goodness.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Human beings possess value because they are created in God's image, loved by God, and offered eternal life through Christ.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains part of Cliffe's uninterrupted opening statement and is framed through his own expressly Christian explanation of human worth.

response.rationale: Constructive opening claim; it supplies a Christian explanation of human value without answering an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances the moral-account route but leaves its grounding largely asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source clearly states the proposed basis of human value, though its exclusively explanatory scope remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The theological explanation is asserted confidently without an argument showing that divine creation is the necessary basis of value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows conditionally from the theological premises, but the bridge from divine regard to objective value is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt cites Jesus's teaching but supplies no independent support for creation, divine love, or their value-conferring force.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Christian moral-account bridge by explaining human worth through the divine image.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own positive account and does not meaningfully interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds value in creation in God's image, divine love, purpose, and the offer of eternal life through Christ.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Objective good and evil require a mind prior to human minds that creates and defines moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement and Cliffe's repeated first-person framing clearly attribute this moral argument to him.

response.rationale: Constructive opening argument; it advances a divine-grounding account rather than responding to an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a recognizable moral argument but compresses its decisive necessity premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but 'real,' 'objective,' and 'creates and defines' are not carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim exceeds the support offered because no rival account of objective normativity is examined.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference depends on an unsupported premise that objective moral facts can exist only if created by a prior mind.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Appeals to conscience support widespread moral experience but do not establish the claimed necessity of a prior defining mind.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely supports the central bridge concerning objective morality within the Christian moral account.

representationalCharity.rationale: No opposing metaethical account is described in enough detail for a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt moves from the speaker's and atheists' consciences to the claim that real good and evil require a mind prior to humanity.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: The resurrection claim should be evaluated through historical and relational evidence, together with logic and reason, rather than through scientific evidence alone.
moves.attributionBasis: Cliffe presents this sustained evidential argument during his uninterrupted opening, with no speaker ambiguity in the delivered rows.

response.rationale: Constructive methodological move; it distinguishes scientific, historical, relational, philosophical, and logical evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes an important methodological distinction, with a bounded application gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The categories and anti-exclusivity claim are clear, though standards appropriate to each category remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It appropriately claims that inquiry must admit multiple evidence types, not that every claimed type proves resurrection.

charity.alternative: Physical resurrection claims remain subject to empirical scrutiny even when known through historical testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: Plural evidence types do not remove the need for evidence appropriate to the physical component of the claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between evidence types coherently defeats scientific exclusivity, though it does not itself validate resurrection evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The love analogy usefully illustrates non-scientific knowledge but only partially supports the historical-resurrection application.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central methodological bridge by defending historical and relational reasoning alongside science.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly limits science's reach but does not expressly preserve empirical scrutiny for a claimed bodily event.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts scientific knowledge with relational knowledge and expressly identifies historical evidence, philosophy, logic, and reason.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A method cannot establish Christianity as true if its consistent application equally verifies mutually incompatible religions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Matt the floor for his opening, and this methodological argument proceeds continuously in Matt's first-person presentation.

components.text: Whether the proposed plurality of evidence supplies a method capable of verifying Christianity rather than incompatible claims.

response.rationale: It contacts the methodological proposal by demanding verification criteria and arguing that symmetric validation of incompatible religions defeats the method's truth-establishing force.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive discriminatory-method issue, though the selected excerpt only begins developing the symmetry test.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional objection clearly concerns methods that validate mutually incompatible claims under consistent application.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for discriminatory verification is proportionate to a debate over whether Christianity is true.

charity.alternative: Different evidence types may legitimately use different standards rather than one universal verification procedure.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those standards must still distinguish Christianity from mutually incompatible claims using the same relevant criteria.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If a method equally verifies contradictions, it cannot by itself establish which incompatible claim corresponds to reality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical symmetry point is strong, though representative rival applications are not developed in the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central-method bridge by requiring truth tests that discriminate among incompatible religions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection permits methodological plurality while retaining the decisive requirement of discriminatory performance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts a correspondence conception of truth and asks how Christianity's defining claims will actually be verified.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Without empirical support for the claimed physical event, a resurrection cannot responsibly be affirmed, and ignorance of a natural explanation does not demonstrate a supernatural one.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt develops this extended epistemic argument without interruption during his opening statement, making the speaker attribution unambiguous.

components.text: Whether historical and relational evidence can warrant affirming a supernatural physical resurrection without empirical support.

response.rationale: It directly challenges the resurrection application by distinguishing lack of a known natural explanation from evidence for a supernatural explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central inferential defect, although it does not evaluate a developed historical case in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between unexplained experience or report and demonstrated supernatural causation is clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker carefully frames the empirical deficit and acknowledges ignorance rather than converting it into certainty about nature.

charity.alternative: Historical testimony could support a unique past physical event even when it cannot be experimentally repeated.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical testimony still must warrant the specifically supernatural inference rather than merely establish an unexplained report.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rejection of an inference from no known natural explanation to supernatural explanation is logically well formed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic distinction is well supported conceptually, with a bounded gap concerning the particulars of resurrection testimony.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con resurrection bridge by attacking the supernatural inference from reported events.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the key testimony question but somewhat compresses how nonrepeatable historical physical claims can be supported.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says reported or experienced events lacking a known natural explanation do not thereby demonstrate anything supernatural.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Jesus's reported death, known burial, postmortem appearances, transformed witnesses, and later conversions constitute a cumulative historical case for his resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle begins by expressly identifying the evidence for the resurrection and then gives a continuous catalogue of supporting claims.

components.text: Whether historical facts and testimony provide positive support rather than merely appealing to ignorance about natural explanations.
Whether the resurrection case supplies specifically Christian evidence capable of discriminating the claim from rivals.

response.rationale: The move offers a positive cumulative historical case—death, burial, appearances, transformations, and conversions—rather than relying solely on absence of a natural explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both demands but only partially answers them because source reliability and comparative alternative analysis remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition and its constituent reported facts are clear, while their historical status is treated implicitly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The resurrection conclusion is stronger than the excerpt's defense of sources, independence, and comparative alternatives permits.

charity.alternative: The cited reports may be sincere or partly historical without establishing bodily resurrection as the best explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cumulative case must defend source reliability and compare ordinary transmission, experience, and body-disposition alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The facts could cumulatively support resurrection, but the bridge to best explanation requires source and alternative-analysis premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move gives specific narrative details but largely treats Gospel reports and witness transformation claims as established historical facts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable pro resurrection bridge through an expressly cumulative historical inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies multiple facts but does not adequately handle the strongest non-resurrection interpretation of those reports.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt begins with Jesus's death, spear wound, burial preparation, and known tomb; the locked proposition adds appearances and transformed witnesses.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even nearly perfect reconstruction and preservation of an original Gospel text would not establish that the claims written in that text correspond to reality.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly discusses the absence of originals, comparison among surviving copies, reconstruction uncertainty, and the separate question of truth.

components.text: Whether accurately transmitted Gospel reports establish that the narrated death, burial, and resurrection events occurred.

response.rationale: It directly separates reconstruction of original wording from correspondence of the original claims to reality, attacking a key documentary warrant.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive transmission-to-truth inference and states the precise limitation of manuscript evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterfactual concession of near-perfect preservation makes the limited conclusion especially clear and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical logical distinction is warranted, while uncertainty about recovering the original is separately acknowledged.

charity.alternative: Reliable preservation can be one component of a broader historical reliability case.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preservation alone establishes what was written, not whether the preserved assertions correspond to reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between textual fidelity and factual correspondence is explicit, valid, and survives the strongest preservation concession.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion is principally conceptual and the manuscript uncertainty is cautiously framed without carrying excessive argumentative weight.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central-documents bridge by separating preservation from truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly grants near-perfect reconstruction and limits only the inference that the concession cannot support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes an almost identical surviving text for argument's sake and denies that this demonstrates the original claims' truth.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Literary form, manuscript preservation, archaeological corroboration, and internal consistency jointly support treating the Gospels as historically reliable.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle explicitly enumerates four tests he applies to historical books and then applies each test to the New Testament Gospels.

components.text: Whether evidence beyond manuscript preservation supports treating the Gospel narratives as historically reliable.
Whether the proposed Gospel tests discriminate factual history from unsupported religious narrative.

response.rationale: It adds literary form, archaeology, and internal consistency to preservation, thereby contacting the demand for a broader truth-sensitive reliability case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive issue but only partially answers it because the criteria's truth-discriminating power is not defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criteria are identifiable, but 'historically reliable' shifts between background accuracy, consistency, and central-event truth.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical denial of contradictions and reliability conclusion exceed the limited evidence shown in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: A narrative can be preserved, internally coherent, and accurate about places while its central events remain untrue.
charity.decisiveQualification: The criteria need an additional warrant connecting those indicators to the truth of the specific supernatural claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Several indicators can support reliability, but the inference equivocates between general historical texture and truth of central claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific categories are named, yet representative archaeological findings, contradiction analysis, and comparative validation are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Gospel bridge by offering a cumulative reliability method.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move adds cumulative indicators but omits the strongest fiction-compatible qualification affecting their probative force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes internal harmony and consistency and concludes that Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John should be read as historically reliable.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Literary style, manuscript preservation, accurate place-names, and internal consistency cannot establish Gospel truth because fictional narratives can satisfy all four criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty systematically follows Knechtle's four stated criteria, tests each criterion, and concludes that the methodology is incapable of establishing truth.

components.text: Whether the four proposed indicators entail or adequately demonstrate the factual truth of the Gospel narrative.

response.rationale: It identifies the inferential failure: fictional narratives can possess each cited property, so the properties do not establish the story's truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies why the offered inference fails and states the defeating consequence for the reliability test.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently targets sufficiency for truth, not the weaker claim that the indicators may carry some evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modal counterexamples justify denying that the four criteria are sufficient to establish factual truth.

charity.alternative: The four indicators may provide cumulative probabilistic support even though none entails truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their probative weight still requires comparative evidence showing they distinguish reliable history from well-formed fiction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Fiction-compatible counterexamples directly defeat the inference from possession of the four properties to factual truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The counterexample structure is strong and specific, with only a bounded gap concerning the criteria's possible probabilistic value.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central documents bridge by testing the truth-discriminating capacity of the proposed criteria.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly defeats sufficiency, though it could more explicitly preserve possible incremental evidential value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt separately explains that accurate places, preserved wording, and appropriate literary style can occur while the story remains false.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Once an offered truth-testing method is shown defective, the critic need not supply a replacement or a method that confirms supernatural claims.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty resumes after the moderator's intervention and directly explains why rebutting Knechtle's method creates no obligation to replace it.

components.text: Whether exposing a defect in the offered reliability method obligates the critic to provide a superior method.

response.rationale: It identifies the burden error and explains that a flawed method is not warranted merely because its critic supplies no replacement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move expressly addresses the replacement demand, diagnoses its burden defect, and gives the consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to a critic who has exposed a defect in an affirmative method.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The burden allocation follows from the expressly stated condition that the offered methodology is flawed.

charity.alternative: A critic's alternative method could help show what standards are feasible and illuminate the dispute.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its usefulness would not make it a prerequisite for rejecting an independently defective affirmative method.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The absence of a replacement does not repair an identified defect in the proponent's method; the inference is explicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: This is chiefly a burden-of-proof argument and needs little external evidence once the methodological defect is assumed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary con burden bridge by rejecting an improper replacement-method requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move correctly distinguishes the affirmative burden from the optional value of proposing alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the critic exposed the methodological problem and is not obliged to fix the foundation of the proponent's beliefs.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: An empty tomb and reported appearances would not alone justify resurrection because late transmitted accounts can acquire embellished details without any conspiracy.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Matt, and the uninterrupted first-person answer continues until the next audience question begins.

components.text: Whether an empty tomb and post-burial appearances are sufficient to justify bodily resurrection as the best explanation.

response.rationale: It grants the core facts conditionally and argues that the specific accounts, their lateness, and possible embellishment must be assessed before resurrection follows.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts sufficiency but develops the embellishment alternative only briefly and without source-specific comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: Conditional phrasing distinguishes granting an empty tomb and appearances from accepting the Gospel accounts' full details.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker cautiously requests account details and offers embellishment as a possibility rather than a demonstrated history.

charity.alternative: Multiple sincere appearance reports plus a known empty tomb could cumulatively favor resurrection over embellishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: That comparison depends on the reports' dates, independence, contents, and transmission history.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion that those facts alone underdetermine resurrection follows, though the embellishment model is only sketched.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general transmission concern is plausible, but the excerpt does not document dating, dependence, or actual embellishment.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con resurrection bridge by challenging the sufficiency of the principal alleged facts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants the proposed facts for argument's sake and identifies the evidential details needed for comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditionally grants a known empty tomb and later sightings, then asks for specific accounts and describes the Gospel story as potentially late and fanciful.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Christian faith calls for evidence-seeking skepticism rather than blind credulity, while inquiry should examine competing accounts of meaning, ethics, and value.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator expressly gives Cliffe the response, after which a continuous answer defines cynicism and skepticism until Matt begins his rebuttal.

components.text: Whether a critic must provide a replacement method after identifying defects in the affirmative methodology.
Whether Christian inquiry should employ hard questions and evidence rather than blind faith.

response.rationale: The praise of evidence-seeking contacts the general method dispute, but labeling a critic cynical for not offering alternatives does not answer the burden-allocation argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant partial answer: it contacts evidential inquiry but misses the decisive no-replacement-burden component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential-skepticism claim is clear, but 'cynic' and 'hyper-skepticism' lack criteria and risk shifting meaning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The call for inquiry is warranted, but the suggestion that critics should supply alternatives is insufficiently qualified.

charity.alternative: A critic may responsibly reject inadequate evidence without offering a complete rival worldview or method.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evidence-seeking skepticism does not itself impose a replacement burden on the critic.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The positive call for skeptical inquiry is coherent, but it does not entail that a critic must state a replacement account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The normative distinction between skepticism and cynicism is asserted without criteria showing the opponent crossed that boundary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Its highest exact contact is an attack on the subsidiary no-replacement-burden bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move weakens the opposing posture by associating nonreplacement with cynicism and omits the decisive burden qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects blind faith, urges hard questions and evidence study, then criticizes someone who shreds beliefs without offering an alternative.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Human beings can have reasons to regard people as meaningful and valuable without belief in God, while textual fidelity does not establish Christianity's truth.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience prompt names Matt, and the ensuing extended answer explicitly discusses Cliffe's four points before ending at the moderator's transition.

components.text: Whether belief in creation in God's image is required for humans to have reasons to regard people as meaningful and valuable.
Whether textual fidelity or authorial intent establishes Christianity's truth.

response.rationale: It directly denies that theistic belief is necessary for human valuation and reiterates that textual fidelity is distinct from truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both issues but only partially answers the value-grounding argument because the secular reasons are not supplied.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modest claim that each side has reasons is clear, though 'meaning and value' covers several distinct concepts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts only the availability of secular reasons, not a fully demonstrated objective grounding.

charity.alternative: The divine-image account aims to ground objective value, not merely report personal reasons for valuing people.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that atheists have reasons for valuing persons does not alone establish an objective secular foundation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It coherently separates actual valuing from theistic belief, but does not fully answer the proposed ontological ground.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The speaker reports having reasons but does not identify or defend them, leaving the affirmative secular account underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con moral-adequacy bridge by presenting secular human valuation as viable.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly denies practical dependence on belief but compresses the stronger objective-grounding interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes authorial intent from truth and states that both speakers possess their own reasons for regarding humans as meaningful and valuable.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Differing Gospel reports are not contradictory when they offer compatible but incomplete perspectives rather than mutually exclusive assertions.
moves.attributionBasis: After the alleged infancy contradiction is presented, Cliffe answers continuously with a two-witness collision analogy before Matt adds agreement.

components.text: Whether apparent differences among Gospel reports necessarily constitute contradictions that undermine reliability.

response.rationale: The collision analogy contacts the consistency issue by showing how differing details can be compatible, but it does not resolve particular Gospel examples or the fiction objection generally.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It partially answers a consistency component while leaving the broader truth-discrimination challenge uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compatibility principle is clear, but its extension from the analogy to all disputed Gospel reports is overbroad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy validly establishes possible compatibility, though any broader no-contradictions conclusion needs case analysis.

charity.alternative: Some differing reports may be mutually exclusive rather than merely complementary selections of detail.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility must be demonstrated for each disputed pair and cannot be inferred from one benign analogy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example successfully proves that difference is not identical to contradiction, with an unproven generalization risk.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy supports the abstract distinction but supplies no representative Gospel comparison establishing actual compatibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Gospel-coherence bridge, though it addresses only one aspect of reliability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately handles compatible omissions but does not address the strongest genuinely exclusive-report alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares two witnesses reporting a scream and screech respectively to illustrate compatible, incomplete perspectives on one collision.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Appeals to creation or divorce do not resolve biblical rules that treat men and women unequally in marriage, remarriage, inheritance, and valuation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly turns back to Knechtle's Matthew 19 answer and advances Dillahunty's previously stated critique of biblical inequality.

components.text: Whether differing narrative details can be compatible rather than contradictory.
Whether the Christian framework consistently sustains equal human value in its treatment of women.

response.rationale: The move does not answer the Gospel-perspective argument, but it bears directly on the earlier human-value claim by citing unequal biblical rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is contrary and issue-bearing toward moral equality but uncontacted as to the schema-selected primary Gospel target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection identifies concrete legal domains and limits its conclusion to unequal treatment under biblical rules.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited asymmetries support unequal legal treatment, though the broader claim about absolute value needs fuller textual demonstration.

charity.alternative: Equal intrinsic value can coexist with differentiated legal roles or historically accommodated rules.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defender must explain why systematic disadvantages do not undermine the claimed normative equality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cited rule asymmetries are relevant counterevidence to a simple claim of scriptural equality, with a remaining worth-role distinction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete legal categories are named, but the selected excerpt does not quote or analyze their underlying texts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con moral-adequacy bridge by testing equal-value claims against biblical provisions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets concrete unequal outcomes, though it only implicitly distinguishes equal worth from identical rules.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies different divorce, remarriage, inheritance, and valuation treatment for men and women and challenges an equality appeal.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Divorce, slavery, polygamy, and sexism reflect accommodation to human hardness rather than God's ideal of equal human value presented before the fall.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle explicitly corrects the characterization of his prior argument and then restates his Genesis-and-fall distinction in a continuous turn.

components.text: Whether unequal biblical practices represent God's normative ideal or accommodation to human wrongdoing.

response.rationale: It directly responds by distinguishing the pre-fall ideal of equal value from later permissions attributed to hardness of heart.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive normative-versus-accommodated distinction but only partially explains the scope and moral limits of accommodation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ideal-accommodation distinction is clear, but extending Jesus's divorce remark to slavery, polygamy, and sexism is insufficiently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited divorce passage does not by itself establish the asserted accommodation account for every listed institution.

charity.alternative: A good deity's regulation of harmful institutions may still create moral responsibility even if those institutions are not ideal.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling a rule accommodation must explain why the permission and its terms were morally justified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Accommodation can reconcile ideal and permission, but the generalization and justification of permitted harms remain missing bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Matthew 19 supports the divorce distinction, while the application to slavery, polygamy, and sexism is mainly asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro subsidiary interpretation bridge by separating divine ideals from accommodated practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the difficult practices but does not address the strongest objection concerning divine authorization and regulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Jesus's hardness-of-heart explanation, labels four practices nonideal, and appeals to Genesis 1–2 for pre-fall equality.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: God's creation of meaningful human freedom permits people to corrupt the good creation, so human atrocities are attributable to human misuse of freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator returns the audience's intervention question to Knechtle, who answers directly using his characteristic free-will defense.

components.text: Whether specific unequal biblical rules are attributable to divine norms or defensible accommodation.

response.rationale: The free-will defense explains human corruption generally but does not answer the challenge concerning rules presented as divinely given in scripture.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies relevant contrary material about human evil but leaves the decisive divine-legislation component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between divine creation and human misuse is clear, though the conditions of meaningful freedom are implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Free will plausibly explains some human evil, but the excerpt does not establish that every cited atrocity follows from it.

charity.alternative: The objection concerns harmful commands or permissions attributed to God, not merely autonomous human wrongdoing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Human freedom does not explain divine endorsement unless the attribution or the moral reason for permission is separately addressed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Free agency coherently permits corruption, but the argument does not connect that defense to allegedly divinely regulated conduct.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possibility of human misuse is plausible, yet no defense is given for libertarian freedom or its full explanatory scope.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the Christian moral account of human wrongdoing, despite weak response to textual morality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move shifts toward human misuse and omits the strongest divine-command component of the opposing objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God created free agents capable of perverting a good creation and attributes extensive corruption to that human capacity.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Exodus prohibits kidnapping rather than slaveholding and, in the same chapter, regulates ownership, unequal release, and violent treatment of slaves.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn immediately answers Knechtle's citation of Exodus 21:16 and uses the detailed textual critique consistently advanced by Dillahunty earlier.

components.text: Whether citing a kidnapping prohibition or nonideal status answers the moral objection to biblical slaveholding regulations.
Whether human misuse alone explains slavery rules contained in a text attributed to divine authority.

response.rationale: It identifies the category error between kidnapping and slaveholding and states that the surrounding chapter affirmatively regulates ownership and unequal treatment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses why the cited prohibition fails and supplies concrete contrary provisions from the same legal context.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes kidnapping from slaveholding and specifies the chapter-level regulatory scope of its objection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical distinction between prohibiting kidnapping and prohibiting slavery is appropriately supported by the cited regulatory context.

charity.alternative: The laws may mitigate an existing institution without expressing God's moral ideal.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mitigation still requires explaining ownership, unequal release, and permitted violence under purported divine legislation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference correctly distinguishes a narrower offense from the broader institution and uses adjacent regulations to defeat equivalence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites several specific features of Exodus, though exact verses and interpretive details are compressed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con moral-adequacy bridge by testing divine goodness against slavery regulations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows that the text can contain a prohibition while showing why it does not resolve the broader regulated-slavery objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes different rules for Jewish slaves, devices for permanent enslavement, unequal release, and the narrow scope of man-stealing.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: The stolen-body hypothesis is implausible because the doubting disciples lacked a credible motive and Jesus's enemies could have produced the body to halt resurrection claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The question explicitly requests Knechtle's evidence, and the ensuing two-pronged historical argument is delivered as one uninterrupted answer.

components.text: Whether a natural body-removal explanation remains credible given disciple motive and the conduct of Jesus's enemies.
Whether rejecting one natural alternative supplies adequate positive warrant for a supernatural resurrection.

response.rationale: It directly challenges theft by disciples or enemies, but does not establish resurrection after excluding only that limited family of alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a material alternative but only partially answers the broader insufficiency and supernatural-inference demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two theft variants are clearly stated, but the conclusion expands from no credible theft to resurrection without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical resurrection conclusion is disproportionate to an argument that addresses only disciple and enemy theft.

charity.alternative: Body removal could involve actors or circumstances other than deliberate theft by believing disciples or hostile authorities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defeating two theft motives does not exclude mistaken tomb identification, relocation, legend, or other transmission alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The motive arguments bear against two theft hypotheses, but the leap from their rejection to resurrection is a false exhaustion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Claims about disciple doubt and enemy incentives are plausible but asserted, and no comprehensive alternative comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro resurrection bridge by comparing resurrection with a named body-removal alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move narrows the alternatives to two weak theft variants and omits other live explanations relevant to the inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that doubting disciples lacked motive to steal the body and enemies would have produced it to stop resurrection preaching.
